note: Evidence examples (9 -> 18): two per capability, one conceptual and one applied. Draft for review.

capabilities.statement: Explain what excelling at university means

evidence.title: What excelling means, explained through deep and surface approaches
evidence.example: You read a short account of deep and surface approaches to learning (Marton and Saljo 1976) and use it to write a paragraph on what excelling at university means: seeking meaning and connecting ideas, not only collecting marks or memorising. You add one example of each approach from your own first weeks. This shows you can explain what excelling involves (for example, a foundation-year design student contrasting copying a tutor's sketch style with understanding why it works).
evidence.artefact: A short written explanation of excelling at university, using deep and surface approaches, with two examples from your own study.
grounding: model: Deep and surface approaches to learning (Marton and Saljo 1976)

evidence.title: Interview with an experienced student about doing well
evidence.example: You interview a second- or third-year student, a student ambassador or your personal tutor about what doing well at university looked like for them, then write a short summary comparing their answer with what you expected from school or college. This shows you can explain what excelling at university means in practice (for example, a criminology student learning that excelling meant reading beyond the list and speaking in seminars, not only grades).
evidence.artefact: Interview notes and a half-page summary comparing your expectations of university with what an experienced student told you.
grounding: practice: conversation with a student ambassador or personal tutor

genericOutcomes.title: Excelling defined through deep and surface learning
genericOutcomes.example: You read a short account of deep and surface approaches to learning and use it to explain what excelling in your studies means: seeking meaning and connecting ideas, not simply collecting marks or memorising facts. You note one moment from your own recent work that fits each approach, then state which one better describes genuine excelling and why. This shows you can define excelling using a recognised distinction rather than a vague impression.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short written explanation of excelling, using the deep and surface distinction, with one example of each.
grounding: model: Deep and surface approaches to learning (Marton and Saljo 1976)

genericOutcomes.title: Interview with a more experienced learner on excelling
genericOutcomes.example: You interview someone further along in their studies about what doing well looked like for them, then write a short summary comparing their answer with what you expected before you started. This shows you can explain what excelling means in practice, for instance discovering that doing well involved reading beyond what was set and contributing actively, not only achieving good results.
genericOutcomes.artefact: Interview notes and a short summary comparing your expectations with what an experienced learner told you.
grounding: professional: Learns what doing well looks like in a role by talking to someone more experienced.

genericOutcomes.title: Excelling characterised through levels of understanding
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can define and explain excelling as a staged progression from meeting minimum requirements to demonstrating mastery, in their own words.
genericOutcomes.example: You set out what excelling in your studies actually involves, using a staged model of understanding that moves from describing isolated facts to relating ideas and finally extending them to new situations. You identify which stage your own recent work has reached and what moving up a stage would look like. This produces a clear, reasoned account of what excelling means, rather than a vague sense of trying harder.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short written account of excelling, naming your current stage of understanding and the next one.
grounding: model: SOLO taxonomy (Biggs and Collis 1982)
benchmark: none (unattributed; written from capability statement)

genericOutcomes.title: Excelling in a role explained to someone new
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can identify and communicate, to someone unfamiliar with a role, the practical difference between adequate performance and excelling, using a concrete example of each.
genericOutcomes.example: You are asked by someone new to a role what doing really well in it looks like, beyond simply meeting the basic requirements. You explain that it means understanding why tasks are done a certain way and connecting them to a bigger purpose, not just completing a checklist. You give one concrete example of each level so the distinction is clear and useful to them.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short explanation given to a newcomer, with one example of basic performance and one of genuine excelling.
grounding: professional: Explains what strong performance in a role looks like to someone new to it.
benchmark: none (unattributed; written from capability statement)

capabilities.statement: Recognise and follow the conventions of academic practice

evidence.title: Own writing annotated as disciplinary practice
evidence.example: You annotate one piece of your writing against your discipline's conventions (referencing style, structure, tone, use of evidence), then explain, using the academic literacies model (Lea and Street 1998), why these are practices of a particular discipline rather than general study skills learned once. This shows you recognising and following the conventions of academic practice (for example, a chemistry student noticing that lab reports use set sections and an impersonal style, unlike an English essay).
evidence.artefact: An annotated piece of your writing marking each convention followed, with a short note on what your discipline expects.
grounding: model: Academic literacies (Lea and Street 1998)

evidence.title: Real document written to an organisation's house style
evidence.example: You find the conventions expected in a setting outside your course, such as a society, volunteering role or part-time job, and compare them with your discipline's. You then follow them in a real task, like writing minutes or a client email. This shows you can recognise and follow conventions when joining a community (for example, a politics student writing their first press release for the students' union in its house style).
evidence.artefact: Your finished document beside the house style guide or template, with a note on the conventions you followed.
grounding: professional: Learns and follows the conventions of a profession or organisation on joining it.

genericOutcomes.title: Own writing annotated against field conventions
genericOutcomes.example: You annotate a piece of your own writing against the conventions typically expected in your field, such as referencing style, structure and tone, then explain why these are practices specific to that field rather than general skills you learn once and apply everywhere. This shows you recognising and following conventions, noticing, for instance, that one type of document uses set sections and an impersonal style while another allows a more personal voice.
genericOutcomes.artefact: An annotated piece of your writing, marking each convention followed and noting what your field expects.
grounding: model: Academic literacies (Lea and Street 1998)

genericOutcomes.title: Document written to match a group's house style
genericOutcomes.example: You find out the conventions expected in a setting outside your usual studies, such as a club, group or role you take part in, and compare them with the ones you already know. You then follow these new conventions in a real task, such as writing minutes or a message on behalf of the group. This shows you can recognise and follow conventions when joining a new community, not only within familiar settings.
genericOutcomes.artefact: Your finished document alongside the style guide or template, with a note on the conventions you followed.
grounding: professional: Learns and follows the conventions of a profession or organisation on joining it.

genericOutcomes.title: Conventions of a field identified before adopting them
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can identify the conventions that govern practice in an unfamiliar field and explain why those conventions exist.
genericOutcomes.example: Before producing a piece of work in an unfamiliar field, you identify the conventions it follows, such as how evidence is presented, what tone is used and how sources are acknowledged, rather than assuming your usual habits will transfer. You explain why these conventions exist for that field specifically. This produces a clear account of recognising conventions as learned practice rather than something fixed or universal across every setting.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short account naming the conventions of an unfamiliar field and explaining why they exist there.
grounding: model: Academic literacies (Lea and Street 1998)
benchmark: none (unattributed; written from capability statement)

genericOutcomes.title: New role's conventions followed from the outset
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can observe and follow the unwritten conventions of a new setting when making their first contributions to it.
genericOutcomes.example: On joining a new team or group, you work out its unwritten conventions, such as how communication is phrased, how decisions are recorded and what tone is expected, by observing before acting and asking when unsure. You then follow these conventions in your own early contributions rather than relying on habits from elsewhere. This shows you recognising and adopting the practices a community expects from someone new to it.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short record of the conventions observed in a new setting and how your first contributions followed them.
grounding: professional: Learns and follows the conventions of a profession or organisation on joining it.
benchmark: none (unattributed; written from capability statement)

capabilities.statement: Adopt a growth mindset towards academic challenge

evidence.title: A setback rewritten in fixed and growth mindset terms
evidence.example: You take a piece of work that went less well than you hoped and write two short accounts of it, one in fixed-mindset terms and one in growth-mindset terms, drawing on Dweck's (2006) distinction between believing ability is fixed and believing it grows with effort and good strategy. You then set one effort-based next step. This shows you adopting a growth mindset towards academic challenge (for example, a mathematics student reframing a low first-term problem sheet mark).
evidence.artefact: Two contrasting reflections on one setback, fixed and growth framed, ending with a concrete next step you then took.
grounding: model: Mindset theory (Dweck 2006)

evidence.title: A stretch challenge taken on with feedback sought midway
evidence.example: You take on a challenge you would usually avoid, such as a hard optional module, a coding competition or a presentation for your society, and ask for feedback partway through. You record what you did with that feedback. This shows you treating difficult work as a chance to learn (for example, a music student entering a composition competition and asking a tutor for comments on a draft score).
evidence.artefact: A record of the challenge, the feedback you asked for and received, and what you changed as a result.
grounding: professional: Treats new and difficult work as a chance to learn and seeks feedback to improve.
professional: Vitae RDF B1: personal qualities

genericOutcomes.title: A setback reframed in fixed and growth terms
genericOutcomes.example: You take a piece of work that went less well than hoped and write two short accounts of it: one assuming your ability is fixed, and one assuming it grows with effort and better strategy. Comparing the two, you set one concrete, effort-based next step. This shows you adopting a growth mindset towards a real setback rather than only towards challenge in the abstract, turning a difficult result into a plan.
genericOutcomes.artefact: Two contrasting reflections on one setback, fixed and growth framed, ending with a concrete next step.
grounding: model: Mindset theory (Dweck 2006)

genericOutcomes.title: A stretch challenge taken on with feedback sought
genericOutcomes.example: You take on a challenge you would normally avoid because it feels too difficult, and partway through you ask someone for feedback on how it is going. You record what the feedback told you and what you changed as a result. This shows you treating difficult work as a chance to learn and improve, rather than avoiding it or waiting until the end to find out whether your approach was working.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A record of the challenge taken on, the feedback sought partway through, and what you changed afterwards.
grounding: professional: Treats new and difficult work as a chance to learn and seeks feedback to improve.

genericOutcomes.title: Challenge reframed as opportunity rather than threat
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can describe how reframing a difficult task as an opportunity to develop a skill reflects a growth mindset.
genericOutcomes.example: Faced with a task that feels beyond your current ability, you deliberately describe it to yourself as an opportunity to build a new skill rather than a test you might fail. You name the specific skill at stake and one small action that would start building it today. This produces a short, honest record of choosing a growth response to challenge instead of avoiding or dismissing it outright.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short written record naming a challenge, the skill at stake, and one action taken today.
grounding: model: Mindset theory (Dweck 2006)
benchmark: none (unattributed; written from capability statement)

genericOutcomes.title: Difficult task treated as a learning opportunity
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can respond to a challenging task by treating it as a chance to learn and acting on feedback received before it is finished.
genericOutcomes.example: Given a task that is harder than anything you have handled before, you choose to treat it as a chance to develop rather than a risk to avoid, and you actively seek feedback while still partway through, not only once it is finished. You note what that feedback let you fix early. This shows you adopting a growth response to challenge in a way that changes the outcome, not just your attitude towards it.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short note on a hard task, the feedback sought midway, and the early fix it allowed.
grounding: professional: Treats new and difficult work as a chance to learn and seeks feedback to improve.
benchmark: none (unattributed; written from capability statement)

evidence.title: Goals rewritten from performance to mastery orientation
evidence.example: You rewrite three of your current goals so they focus on mastery (understanding or skill) rather than performance (beating others or just reaching a grade), using Pintrich's (2000) mastery and performance goal orientations. You track progress against them for a month and note what kept you going. This shows you setting and sustaining mastery-oriented goals (for example, a physiotherapy student turning 'get 70 in anatomy' into 'explain the muscles of the shoulder without notes').
evidence.artefact: Original and rewritten goals with each orientation labelled, plus a month of dated progress notes.
grounding: ing:doc:self-regulated-learning-goal-orientation-pintrich-2000

evidence.title: Development goal pursued in a coaching or work role
evidence.example: In a part-time job, sports club or volunteering role, you set yourself a development goal beyond the targets you are given and work towards it over a term, reviewing it with a supervisor or coach. This shows you can set and sustain a mastery goal outside the classroom (for example, a sport science student coaching a youth team who sets out to learn to plan a full training session, not just run drills).
evidence.artefact: A goal statement, termly review notes and a short comment from your supervisor or coach on your progress.
grounding: professional: Sets development goals beyond targets and keeps working towards them.
professional: Vitae RDF B2: self-management

genericOutcomes.title: Goals rewritten from performance to mastery focus
genericOutcomes.example: You take three goals you are currently working towards and rewrite each so it focuses on mastery, understanding or genuine skill, rather than on performance, such as beating others or simply hitting a target grade. Over the following month you track your progress against the rewritten goals and note what kept you working at them. This shows you setting and sustaining mastery-oriented goals rather than ones driven mainly by comparison or marks.
genericOutcomes.artefact: Original and rewritten goals with each orientation labelled, plus a month of dated progress notes.
grounding: ing:doc:self-regulated-learning-goal-orientation-pintrich-2000

genericOutcomes.title: Development goal pursued beyond what was set
genericOutcomes.example: In a role outside your formal studies, such as a club, team or part-time position, you set yourself a development goal that goes beyond the targets you have been given, and you work towards it over several weeks, reviewing progress with someone who oversees your work there. This shows you can set and sustain a mastery goal in a real setting, not only when a goal is handed to you.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A goal statement, dated progress notes and a short comment from someone overseeing your work.
grounding: professional: Sets development goals beyond targets and keeps working towards them.
professional: Vitae RDF B2: self-management

genericOutcomes.title: A mastery goal set and tracked over time
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can analyse the difference between a mastery goal and a performance target, and define what achieving a mastery goal would involve.
genericOutcomes.example: You set yourself one goal defined purely in terms of understanding or capability, rather than a mark or an external target, and you write down in advance what achieving it would actually look like. Over several weeks you log short, dated notes on your progress and what kept you committed when motivation dipped. This produces a clear, dated record of pursuing mastery deliberately rather than drifting towards whatever is simply easiest to measure.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A mastery goal statement with weekly dated progress notes and a comment on sustained motivation.
grounding: ing:doc:self-regulated-learning-goal-orientation-pintrich-2000
benchmark: none (unattributed; written from capability statement)

genericOutcomes.title: A mastery goal sustained in a real role
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can set a mastery goal that goes beyond required targets and sustain progress towards it over time without external prompting.
genericOutcomes.example: In a role where you are given set targets, you additionally set yourself a mastery goal that goes beyond what is measured, such as deepening a skill rather than hitting a quota, and you keep working at it even when no one is checking. You review your own progress at set intervals and record what sustained your effort. This shows you can set and sustain a mastery goal unprompted, in a live setting with real demands.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A mastery goal set in a real role, with interval reviews and a note on sustained effort.
grounding: professional: Sets development goals beyond targets and keeps working towards them.
benchmark: none (unattributed; written from capability statement)

capabilities.statement: Build self-efficacy and manage stress and anxiety under pressure

evidence.title: Confidence plan built on four sources of self-efficacy
evidence.example: You plan how to build confidence for an assessment you find daunting, using Bandura's (1977) four sources of self-efficacy: mastery experiences, vicarious experience, verbal persuasion, and physiological and emotional states. You choose one action under each, carry them out and evaluate which made most difference. This shows you building self-efficacy and managing stress under pressure (for example, an education student preparing for a first micro-teaching session by rehearsing short sections, watching peers and calming nerves beforehand).
evidence.artefact: A four-source self-efficacy plan with the actions you took and a short evaluation of which helped most.
grounding: model: Sources of self-efficacy (Bandura 1977)

evidence.title: Stress and coping log across a real deadline cluster
evidence.example: During a high-pressure period, such as a cluster of deadlines or a placement assessment, you keep a brief stress log and use chosen strategies (planning, sleep, talking to someone, short breaks) to stay on track. Afterwards you review what kept your confidence and performance steady. This shows you managing stress under real pressure (for example, a journalism student meeting deadlines on the student newspaper during exam season).
evidence.artefact: A dated stress and coping log across the pressured period, with a short end-of-period review.
grounding: professional: Keeps confidence and performance under pressure and copes with stress.
professional: Tomlinson (2017): psychological capital

genericOutcomes.title: Confidence plan built on four sources of self-efficacy
genericOutcomes.example: You plan how to build confidence for a task you find daunting, using four recognised sources of self-efficacy: direct experience of succeeding at it, watching someone similar succeed, encouragement from others, and managing how nervous or calm you feel. You take one action under each source, then evaluate afterwards which made the most difference. This shows you building self-efficacy and managing pressure using a structured plan, not just hoping nerves settle.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A four-source self-efficacy plan with the actions taken and a short evaluation of what helped most.
grounding: model: Sources of self-efficacy (Bandura 1977)

genericOutcomes.title: Stress and coping log kept across a pressured period
genericOutcomes.example: During a genuinely high-pressure period, such as several deadlines landing close together, you keep a brief daily log of your stress levels and the coping strategies you use, such as planning ahead, protecting sleep, talking to someone, or taking short breaks. Afterwards you review which strategies actually kept your confidence and performance steady. This shows you managing stress under real, sustained pressure rather than only describing strategies you intend to use.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A dated stress and coping log across the pressured period, with a short end-of-period review.
grounding: professional: Keeps confidence and performance under pressure and copes with stress.
professional: Tomlinson (2017): psychological capital

genericOutcomes.title: Independent working planned to manage pressure
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can explain how structuring independent work into manageable stages helps sustain confidence and reduce stress under pressure.
genericOutcomes.example: You take full responsibility for managing a demanding piece of work without relying on someone else to structure it for you, and you deliberately build in strategies that keep your confidence steady, such as breaking the task into stages you know you can complete and tracking small wins along the way. You record how working independently in this planned way changed your stress levels compared with previous, less structured attempts. This demonstrates managing your own learning under pressure.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short record showing how working independently, staged into small wins, kept confidence steady under pressure.
grounding: model: Sources of self-efficacy (Bandura 1977)
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/independent-and-self-directed-learning

genericOutcomes.title: Confidence sustained while working independently under pressure
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can manage their own learning independently under pressure, adjusting their approach when they notice confidence or stress levels changing.
genericOutcomes.example: Given a task to manage on your own, with a genuine deadline and no one checking your progress day to day, you set up your own structure for staying on track and your own way of noticing early if stress is building. You adjust your approach partway through when you notice confidence dipping, rather than waiting for someone else to intervene. This shows you managing your own learning and performance under pressure, independently and effectively.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short account of adjusting your own approach midway through independent, pressured work to protect confidence.
grounding: professional: Keeps confidence and performance under pressure and copes with stress.
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/independent-and-self-directed-learning

capabilities.statement: Develop an academic voice and the confidence to own one's practice

evidence.title: Early and recent writing compared for authorial voice
evidence.example: You compare an early and a recent piece of your writing using Ivanič's (1998) idea of writer identity, especially the self as author: how far you state your own position and stand behind your claims. You annotate where your voice is stronger and explain the choices you made within the discipline's conventions. This shows you developing an academic voice and owning your practice (for example, a sociology student moving from summarising sources to arguing a position on them).
evidence.artefact: Two annotated extracts, early and recent, with a commentary on how your authorial voice has developed.
grounding: model: Writer identity and self as author (Ivanič 1998)

evidence.title: Own view presented and defended at a student conference
evidence.example: You present and defend your own view in a real setting beyond the module, such as a departmental seminar, an undergraduate research conference or a course representative meeting, and handle questions on it. This shows the confidence to own your practice in your own voice (for example, an anthropology student presenting fieldwork findings at a student conference and answering challenge from staff).
evidence.artefact: Your abstract or slides, the questions you were asked and a short reflection on how you responded.
grounding: professional: Speaks and writes with a professional voice and owns their practice within the profession's standards.

genericOutcomes.title: Writing voice compared across early and recent work
genericOutcomes.example: You compare an early piece of your writing with a recent one, focusing on how far each states your own position and stands behind its claims rather than only summarising what others have said. You annotate where your voice is stronger in the later piece and explain the specific choices behind that shift. This shows you developing a distinct voice and the confidence to own your own views within accepted conventions.
genericOutcomes.artefact: Two annotated extracts, early and recent, with a commentary on how your authorial voice developed.
grounding: model: Writer identity and self as author (Ivanič 1998)

genericOutcomes.title: Your own view presented and defended publicly
genericOutcomes.example: You present your own view in a real setting beyond your usual coursework, such as an open talk, a panel or a group meeting, stating a position clearly and backing it with reasons rather than simply reporting what others think. You then handle questions and challenge on the spot. This shows the confidence to own your practice and voice in front of others, under genuine scrutiny rather than in a safely private draft.
genericOutcomes.artefact: Your notes or slides, the questions you were asked, and a short reflection on your responses.
grounding: professional: Speaks and writes with a professional voice and owns their practice within the profession's standards.

genericOutcomes.title: Voice grounded in command of core content
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can distinguish their own interpretation of a topic from paraphrased source material, grounding that interpretation in broad, well-founded subject knowledge.
genericOutcomes.example: You take a topic you know well and write a short piece stating your own interpretation of it, deliberately drawing on your broad, well-founded grasp of the core material to support claims you make in your own words, rather than paraphrasing a single source. You mark the sentences where the view is distinctly yours. This demonstrates a voice that stands on solid knowledge rather than borrowed phrasing or secondhand opinion.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short piece on a familiar topic with your own sentences marked as distinct from paraphrased source material.
grounding: model: Writer identity and self as author (Ivanič 1998)
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/subject-knowledge-and-understanding

genericOutcomes.title: Expert view voiced with confidence in practice
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can voice their own professional assessment of a situation, drawing on well-founded subject knowledge, and defend that assessment when questioned.
genericOutcomes.example: Drawing on your broad, well-founded knowledge of a subject, you give your own assessment of a situation to colleagues or peers, rather than simply relaying facts, and you stand behind that assessment when it is questioned. You note afterwards which parts of your knowledge let you speak with genuine confidence and which parts you still need to strengthen. This shows the confidence to own a professional view grounded in real command of the material.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short record of an assessment you gave and defended, and the knowledge gaps it revealed.
grounding: professional: Speaks and writes with a professional voice and owns their practice within the profession's standards.
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/subject-knowledge-and-understanding

capabilities.statement: Articulate one's graduate capital for the move from student to graduate

evidence.title: Graduate capital audit across Tomlinson's five forms
evidence.example: You audit yourself against Tomlinson's (2017) graduate capital model, covering human, social, cultural, identity and psychological capital, finding evidence for each from your degree, work and activities and naming the weakest form. You then write a short plan to strengthen it. This shows you can articulate your graduate capital for the move from student to graduate (for example, an engineering student finding strong technical knowledge but few industry contacts, so weak social capital).
evidence.artefact: A five-part graduate capital audit with evidence under each form and a plan for the weakest one.
grounding: model: Graduate capital model (Tomlinson 2017)

evidence.title: Graduate capital evidenced in a real application or mock interview
evidence.example: You use your capital audit in a real application or a mock interview with the careers service, giving evidence-backed answers on your knowledge, networks, fit, identity and resilience, then ask for feedback. This shows you can present your graduate capital to an employer (for example, a history student applying for a heritage trainee scheme and using museum volunteering as evidence).
evidence.artefact: A submitted application or recorded mock interview, with the careers adviser's feedback and your revisions.
grounding: professional: Presents own knowledge, networks, cultural fit, professional identity and resilience to an employer, with evidence.
professional: Tomlinson (2017): graduate capital

genericOutcomes.title: Personal capital audited across five recognised forms
genericOutcomes.example: You audit yourself against a recognised model of the capital that supports a move into a career, covering knowledge, networks, cultural fit, identity and resilience, finding evidence for each from your studies, work and activities, and naming the weakest form. You then write a short plan to strengthen it. This shows you can articulate your own capital for the transition ahead, rather than relying on a vague sense of being ready or not.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A five-part capital audit with evidence under each form and a plan for the weakest one.
grounding: model: Graduate capital model (Tomlinson 2017)

genericOutcomes.title: Capital evidenced in a real application
genericOutcomes.example: You use your capital audit when putting together a genuine application or going into a mock interview, giving evidence-backed answers about your knowledge, networks, fit, identity and resilience rather than generic statements, then you ask for feedback on how convincing those answers were. You revise at least one answer in light of that feedback. This shows you presenting your own capital to someone making a real judgement about your readiness.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A submitted application or recorded mock interview, with the feedback received and your revisions.
grounding: professional: Presents own knowledge, networks, cultural fit, professional identity and resilience to an employer, with evidence.
professional: Tomlinson (2017): graduate capital

genericOutcomes.title: Readiness for transition mapped across personal assets
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can synthesise distinct forms of personal advantage, such as knowledge, networks and resilience, into a reasoned account of their readiness for transition.
genericOutcomes.example: You list the distinct kinds of advantage you bring into your next step, such as what you know, who you know, how well you fit a new setting, how you see yourself, and how well you cope with setbacks, and you find one piece of concrete evidence for each. You then rank them from strongest to weakest and explain why. This produces a reasoned map of your own readiness rather than a single, vague impression of confidence.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A ranked list of five kinds of personal advantage, each backed by one piece of evidence.
grounding: model: Graduate capital model (Tomlinson 2017)
benchmark: none (unattributed; written from capability statement)

genericOutcomes.title: Personal advantages presented to a decision-maker
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can justify their readiness for a genuine transition by presenting specific personal advantages, each supported by evidence, to a decision-maker.
genericOutcomes.example: In a real conversation where someone is deciding whether to take you on, such as for a role, a place or a position of responsibility, you lay out the specific advantages you bring, backed by one concrete example for each, rather than listing generic strengths. You ask directly which of these landed most convincingly and which needs stronger evidence. This shows you can articulate your readiness for a genuine transition under real scrutiny.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short record of advantages presented in a real decision conversation and which landed most convincingly.
grounding: professional: Presents own knowledge, networks, cultural fit, professional identity and resilience to an employer, with evidence.
benchmark: none (unattributed; written from capability statement)

capabilities.statement: Direct one's own learning and development, as a lifelong learner

evidence.title: Post-degree development plan grounded in andragogy
evidence.example: You write a development plan for the year after your degree, using Knowles's (1980) andragogy, with its view of the adult learner as self-directing, to justify how you will identify your own needs, choose resources and judge your progress without a module to set them. This shows you directing your own learning and development (for example, a computing student planning how to learn a new programming framework through online courses and contributions to an open-source project).
evidence.artefact: A post-degree development plan stating needs, chosen resources, milestones and how you will review your own progress.
grounding: model: Andragogy (Knowles 1980)

evidence.title: Self-directed learning to close a career-relevant gap
evidence.example: You identify a gap that your course does not cover but your intended career needs, then plan and complete the learning yourself, such as a short online course, a professional body module or a side project, and record it as continuing development. This shows you directing your learning independently (for example, a psychology student completing an introductory course in data analysis software before applying for research assistant roles).
evidence.artefact: A continuing development record entry: the gap, the learning completed, a certificate or output, and how you used it.
grounding: professional: Directs own practice, learning and development independently throughout a career.
professional: Vitae RDF B3: professional and career development

genericOutcomes.title: Development plan grounded in adult-learning theory
genericOutcomes.example: You write a plan for the period right after you finish your current programme of study, drawing on a recognised view of adult learners as self-directing, to justify how you will identify your own needs, choose your own resources and judge your own progress without a formal course setting these for you. This shows you directing your own learning and development as a matter of deliberate design, not simply drifting once formal structure disappears.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A development plan stating your needs, chosen resources, milestones and how you will review progress.
grounding: model: Andragogy (Knowles 1980)

genericOutcomes.title: A learning gap closed through self-directed study
genericOutcomes.example: You identify something your formal studies did not cover but that the path you want to follow genuinely needs, then you plan and complete that learning yourself, such as a short course, a module from a professional body, or a self-set project, and you keep a record of it as ongoing development. This shows you directing your own learning independently, closing a real gap rather than waiting for someone else to set the task.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A development record entry: the gap identified, the learning completed, and how you used it.
grounding: professional: Directs own practice, learning and development independently throughout a career.
professional: Vitae RDF B3: professional and career development

genericOutcomes.title: Own learning managed without external direction
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can construct a self-directed plan for a substantial piece of learning, justifying the sources, sequence and standard of knowledge chosen without external direction.
genericOutcomes.example: You take full ownership of a substantial piece of learning that nobody else has structured for you: you decide what to learn, in what order, from which sources, and how you will know when you have learned it well enough. You carry this through to completion and keep a short log of the decisions you made along the way and why. This demonstrates managing your own learning and working independently, with no one setting the steps for you.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A decision log for a self-structured piece of learning, from start to completed, independent outcome.
grounding: model: Andragogy (Knowles 1980)
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/independent-and-self-directed-learning

genericOutcomes.title: Independent work carried through unprompted and unsupervised
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can independently plan, carry out and judge the standard of a substantial piece of work, directing their own learning without external oversight.
genericOutcomes.example: At work, you take on a substantial task where no one tells you how to proceed, and you independently plan the steps, find what you need to complete it, and judge for yourself when it is done to a good standard. You keep a short account of the decisions you made without waiting to be told. This shows you managing your own learning and work independently, under real conditions with no one checking each step.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short account of an independently planned and completed work task, with no step checked beforehand.
grounding: professional: Directs own practice, learning and development independently throughout a career.
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/independent-and-self-directed-learning

evidence.title: Reflective essay tracing your path towards self-authorship
evidence.example: You write a reflective essay tracing your journey towards self-authorship (Baxter Magolda 2001), from relying on others' formulas for what to think and do towards defining your own beliefs, identity and commitments. You use specific moments from your studies as evidence and say what kind of graduate you have become. This shows you consolidating a graduate identity (for example, a master's student in social policy describing how a dissertation on housing changed the work they want to do).
evidence.artefact: A reflective essay of about 1,500 words on your development towards self-authorship, citing dated moments from your studies.
grounding: model: Self-authorship (Baxter Magolda 2001)

evidence.title: Professional profile tested with a practitioner in the field
evidence.example: You write a professional profile or personal statement for a real next step, such as a job, a doctoral application or professional registration, presenting a coherent account of who you are as a graduate, and test it with someone working in that field. This shows a consolidated graduate identity that others can recognise (for example, an architecture master's student revising their portfolio statement after a practice director's comments).
evidence.artefact: Your profile or statement, the practitioner's comments and your revised version.
grounding: practice: application for employment, further study or professional registration

genericOutcomes.title: Reflective account tracing a path to self-authorship
genericOutcomes.example: You write a reflective account tracing your own journey towards defining what you believe, who you are and what you are committed to, rather than continuing to rely on other people's formulas for what to think and do. You use specific, dated moments from your studies as evidence and state what kind of graduate you have become as a result. This shows you consolidating a graduate identity through deliberate, evidenced reflection rather than vague self-description.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A reflective account of about a thousand words on your development, citing dated moments from your studies.
grounding: model: Self-authorship (Baxter Magolda 2001)

genericOutcomes.title: Professional profile tested with someone established
genericOutcomes.example: You write a short profile or personal statement for a genuine next step, such as applying for a role or a further place of study, presenting a coherent account of who you are as a graduate, and you test it with someone already established in that field. This shows a consolidated graduate identity that other people can recognise and respond to, rather than one that only makes sense to you, and you revise it based on their comments.
genericOutcomes.artefact: Your profile or statement, the comments you received and your revised version.
grounding: professional: Presents a coherent account of oneself as a graduate that others in the field can recognise and test.

genericOutcomes.title: Identity grounded in command of core knowledge
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can critique their own development by linking specific, well-founded subject knowledge to an emerging sense of themselves as a graduate.
genericOutcomes.example: You write a short account of who you are becoming, as shown through the breadth and depth of what you now know in your field, picking out the core knowledge you can draw on confidently and without notes. You connect specific pieces of that knowledge to how you now see yourself and what you want to do with it. This demonstrates an identity consolidated through genuine command of subject matter, not borrowed labels or titles.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short written account linking specific core knowledge to how you now see yourself as a graduate.
grounding: model: Self-authorship (Baxter Magolda 2001)
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/subject-knowledge-and-understanding

genericOutcomes.title: Graduate identity shown through command of knowledge
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can present themselves to others as a graduate by drawing fluently on well-founded subject knowledge rather than listing qualifications alone.
genericOutcomes.example: In a conversation with someone outside your studies, such as at an event or a first meeting in a new role, you describe yourself as a graduate by drawing directly on the broad, well-founded knowledge you now hold, rather than listing qualifications alone. You notice which parts of that knowledge you can speak about with real fluency and confidence. This shows a graduate identity grounded in substance, recognisable to someone meeting you for the first time.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short reflection on describing yourself as a graduate through knowledge rather than qualifications alone.
grounding: professional: Presents a coherent account of oneself as a graduate that others in the field can recognise and test.
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/subject-knowledge-and-understanding
